svg.text: After the disaster: what actually kills people in the weeks that follow
The deaths from the event itself are only the first wave
In a flood or displacement in Ghana, more people are lost to what comes AFTER than to the water itself:
cholera and other diarrhoeal disease · measles in crowded shelters · malaria · untreated chronic illness
because the medicines were left behind · malnutrition in young children · and unattended births.
Priorities in a relief camp, in order
1 Safe water and sanitation
2 Shelter and warmth
3 Food and nutrition screening
4 Measles vaccination and vitamin A
5 Disease surveillance and case finding
Why water comes before everything
Crowding plus contaminated water plus poor
sanitation produces cholera within days.
Free residual chlorine 0.2 to 0.5 mg/L routinely,
and at least 0.5 mg/L during an outbreak.
Latrines sited away from and downhill of any
water source. Handwashing points at every latrine.
Two things that go wrong in every response
DEAD BODIES DO NOT CAUSE EPIDEMICS. This is the most persistent myth in disaster work. Bodies of people
killed by trauma pose almost no infection risk. Handle them with dignity, identify them, and never rush mass
burial — unidentified burial causes families years of anguish and blocks inheritance and remarriage.
RUMOUR SPREADS FASTER THAN DISEASE. Give the community accurate information early and repeatedly,
through people they already trust — chiefs, imams, pastors, assembly members — not only through officials.
